name: LTC3805IMSE-5#TRPBF
title: Current-mode DC/DC controller for flyback, boost and SEPIC converters, with adjustable frequency
summary: The LTC3805-5 is a peak current-mode PWM controller that drives an external N-channel MOSFET in flyback, boost and SEPIC converters. One resistor sets the frequency from 70kHz to 700kHz, and the part can lock to an external clock; slope compensation and the overcurrent trip are set by resistors, and one capacitor sets soft-start and the automatic restart delay. It runs from 4.7V to 8.8V on VCC, or from a high input through a resistor using its 9.5V shunt clamp, drawing 360µA in operation and 40µA at start-up. The converter's input and output voltages are limited only by the external parts. It comes in a 10-lead MSOP with exposed pad and a 3mm × 3mm DFN.

notes: All are lead-free finish. The grade letter (E, I, H, MP) sets the guaranteed temperature range; the grade is shown on a label on the shipping container.

circuits.title: 5V to 12V/1A Boost Converter
circuits.description: A 5 V rail stepped up to 12 V at up to 1 A. The controller runs from the input itself: VCC and RUN both sit on the 5 V input, so the VCC lockout decides when it starts. GATE drives the N-channel switch; the 8 mΩ resistor in its source is the current sense, read by ISENSE through 3 kΩ (which with the internal ramp current sets slope compensation) and by OC through 1.33 kΩ (which lowers the overcurrent trip). The 191 k / 13.7 k divider returns 12 V to FB, 20 k with 470 pF compensates ITH, 0.1 µF on SSFLT sets soft-start and fault timeout, and 118 k on FS sets the switching frequency. SYNC is grounded.

circuits.title: Figure 8. 5.5V to 40V to 12V/2A SEPIC Converter
circuits.description: A SEPIC that holds 12 V at 2 A from an input anywhere between 5.5 V and 40 V. T1 is a coupled inductor (4.56 µH, BH510-1009): its first winding runs from the input to the switch drain, a 10 µF 50 V capacitor couples the drain to the second winding, and D1 rectifies into a 47 µF output. VCC is fed two ways: at start-up an NPN follower whose base is held by a 6.8 V Zener (57.6 k from the input) charges the 4.7 µF VCC capacitor; once running, the 12 V output feeds VCC through a BAS516 diode and 301 Ω. RUN is divided from the input by 221 k / 69.8 k. R3 100 k and R4 7.15 k set the output. ITH has 10 k in series with 6.8 nF to ground plus a second capacitor directly to ground; 0.1 µF on SSFLT; 80.6 k on FS. The 5 mΩ sense resistor goes straight to OC and to ISENSE through 3.01 k. SYNC is left open.

parts.note: coupled inductor; pins P1 (dotted) and P2 are the first winding, S1 (dotted) and S2 the second

circuits.title: Figure 9. Isolated Telecom Supply: 18V to 72V Input to 3.3V/3A Output
circuits.description: An isolated flyback giving 3.3 V at 3 A from an 18 V to 72 V telecom input. On the primary, a PA1277NL transformer (primary pins 4 and 3, bias winding pins 2 and 1) is switched by an FDC2512 with a 0.04 Ω sense resistor; 150 pF 200 V in series with 68 Ω snubs the drain. An MMBTA42 follower with its base on a 6.8 V Zener (221 k from the input) brings VCC up at start, a second 221 k also feeds VCC from the input, and the bias winding then supplies VCC through 402 Ω (RBIAS) and a BAS516. FB is grounded and the loop is closed on ITH instead: the PS2801-1-K opto-coupler transistor, pulled up to VCC by 6.8 k, pulls ITH down through a Schottky diode. OC and SYNC are grounded; ISENSE reads the sense resistor through 3.01 k. On the secondary, windings 5-6 and 7-8 feed the 3.3 V output with D1 (PDS1040) in the return leg and three 100 µF 6.3 V capacitors. An LT4430 opto driver, powered from the secondary through 10 Ω and a BAS516 and from the output through a BA760, compares the 100 k / 22.1 k divider at FB and drives the opto LED through 274 Ω and a BAS516; 2.2 nF with 56 k compensates COMP, 47 pF bypasses the upper divider resistor, and 0.47 µF sits on its OC pin. 2200 pF 250 VAC joins the two grounds across the barrier.

circuits.title: 5V to 40V to 12V/1A Nonisolated Flyback Converter
circuits.description: A flyback giving 12 V at 1 A from 5 V to 40 V, with the output returned to the input ground. The T3772 transformer's primary (pins 4 and 1) is switched by an FDC2512 with a 5 mΩ sense resistor; 150 pF 200 V with 220 Ω snubs the drain. Secondary windings 7-8 and 10-9 feed a UPS840 Schottky and two 100 µF 16 V capacitors. An MMBTA42 follower, base on a 6.8 V Zener fed by 10 k from the input, charges the 4.7 µF VCC capacitor at start; the bias winding then supplies VCC through a BAS516 and 680 Ω. RUN is tied to VCC, so the VCC lockout gates operation. 51.1 k / 3.65 k sets 12 V at FB with 47 pF across the upper resistor. ITH has 20 k in series with 470 pF, plus 100 pF, to ground; CSS 0.1 µF on SSFLT; 75 k on FS. OC goes straight to the sense resistor and ISENSE through 3.01 k. SYNC is grounded.

parts.note: transformer; pins 4-1 primary (1 dotted), 7, 8 (dotted) and 10, 9 secondary, B1 (dotted) and B2 the bias winding, whose pins carry no number

operation.text: Fixed-frequency peak current-mode control. At the start of each cycle the oscillator sets an SR latch and GATE turns the external MOSFET on. Current in the switch builds a voltage across the source sense resistor; when the ISENSE voltage exceeds a level set by the ITH voltage, the current comparator resets the latch and the switch turns off. If the comparator never trips, the duty cycle is cut off at 80%. FB goes to a transconductance error amplifier against an 800mV reference; a falling output pulls FB low, the amplifier sources current into ITH, ITH rises and so does the peak current. A series RC from ITH to ground compensates the loop and largely sets its response to line and load steps. No pin has to touch the converter's input or output voltage, so those can exceed the part's own ratings.

Two conditions must both be met to run: VCC above VTURNON (4.5V typ) and RUN above VRUNON (1.207V typ). Running stops when VCC falls below VTURNOFF (about 4V) or RUN falls below VRUNOFF (1.170V typ); an overcurrent fault (OC above 100mV) moves the part into fault timeout, which passes to shutdown once SSFLT has discharged below 0.7V. In shutdown the part draws about 40µA. RUN has 35mV of built-in hysteresis, and while running it sources 5µA, which adds hysteresis through the divider's Thevenin resistance. RUN may instead be tied to VCC, leaving the VCC thresholds in control.
A small N-channel MOSFET from RUN to GND stops the converter when its gate is driven high.

RFS from FS to ground sets 70kHz to 700kHz. A clock on SYNC starts each cycle on its rising edge (GATE goes high); its pulse width is not critical. The clock must lie within ±33% of the RFS-set frequency and between 70kHz and 700kHz, with at least 2.9V amplitude.

At high load ITH clamps near 1.9V, which caps the ISENSE voltage at 100mV and limits the peak switch current cycle by cycle while the output sags. Further load pushes the duty cycle down to its 6% minimum, after which the comparator can no longer limit the current. OC, also on the sense resistor, trips a fault at 100mV: the part shuts down, waits out the fault timeout and restarts, repeating (hiccup) for as long as the fault persists. A 10µA current out of OC lets a series resistor ROC lower the trip point; ROC = 0 trips near minimum duty cycle (about 6%). Two sense resistors or a small divider across the sense resistor raise the trip point instead. Overcurrent can also trip during start-up while large output capacitors charge, or during a load step; a larger SSFLT capacitor slows the output rise.

With SSFLT open, internal timers give about 1.8ms soft-start and about 4.25ms fault timeout; these are minimums. A capacitor CSS on SSFLT lengthens both: on leaving shutdown CSS is charged quickly to about 0.7V, where switching starts; a 6µA current then ramps it to about 2.25V, where soft-start ends and closed-loop regulation takes over; it then charges on to about 4.75V. After a fault, 2µA discharges CSS from 4.75V to 0.7V before a restart is attempted.

ISENSE sources a current ramp that starts at zero once the switch has been on for the 6% minimum duty cycle and rises roughly linearly to 10µA at 80%, stopping when GATE falls. A resistor RSLOPE between ISENSE and the sense resistor turns it into a voltage that adds to the sense signal, lowering the current limit in proportion to duty cycle and preventing subharmonic oscillation.

An internal shunt regulator, active even in shutdown, clamps VCC at about 9.5V while sinking up to 25mA, so VCC can be fed from a high voltage through a resistor RVCC from VIN, at the cost of the resistor's loss and a limit on the input range set by the 25mA maximum. VCC may also be driven from a low-impedance source of 4.7V to 8.8V. VCC needs at least 1µF ceramic or tantalum right at the VCC and GND pins to carry the gate driver's current pulses. In a flyback, a bias winding can supply VCC, with an NPN follower and Zener speeding the initial rise and allowing a smaller VCC capacitor; VCC then tracks the regulated output loosely. A resistor RBIAS limits current if the winding gives too much voltage.

Input and output voltage are bounded only by the power components: the MOSFET's BVDSS, RDS(ON) and drain current, the transformer's saturation flux and insulation, the capacitors' voltage, ESR and ripple current ratings, and the rectifier and sense resistor power ratings.

Because the divider sets the output, the turns ratio is free to choose, for example from the wanted duty cycle; small-integer ratios suit off-the-shelf parts. The input voltage plus the reflected secondary flyback voltage, leakage spike included, must stay below the MOSFET breakdown. Leakage inductance causes a drain spike after turn-off that grows with load and may need an RC snubber; bifilar winding reduces leakage but lowers primary-to-secondary breakdown.

In isolated designs FB is grounded, which pulls ITH up, and an opto-coupler on the far side of the barrier pulls ITH down. The opto is biased by a resistor to VCC, and since ITH cannot sink that current, a low-leakage Schottky or low-drop PN diode separates them so the opto can pull ITH to its lower clamp.

Sense values between a few ohms and some tens of milliohms set peak currents between well under one amp and several amps. With 100mV, 5A peak needs 0.020Ω, which dissipates 0.5W at the peak. There is a single sense connection, so ground-side trace and via resistance adds to the sense value: 1mΩ extra on 0.020Ω lowers the peak current by 5%.
